extracted.intended_audience: historians, students, and practitioners interested in North-West Mounted Police / frontier policing history and operational norms
extracted.subtask_description: Operational, organisational and ethical standards for the North‑West Mounted Police (late 19th / early 20th century) covering duties, equipment, public health, investigations, patrol conduct and personnel recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain unit identity to preserve esprit de corps
rubrics_metrics.description: "If ever there should be another war... Canada should strive to have her units kept intact. Destruction of identity leads to destruction of great traditions... and to the loss of the esprit de corps and noblesse oblige elements, which go so far to creating unconquerable regiments."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy guidance: keep formations and units intact when deploying so traditions, unit pride and effectiveness are preserved. Anti-pattern: dissolving or anonymizing units in theatre resulting in loss of identity and morale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valor and self‑sacrifice in combat
rubrics_metrics.description: Exemplified by acts such as Sergeant A. H. L. Richardson riding back under cross‑fire to retrieve a wounded man and accounts of officers attempting to rescue comrades despite grave danger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational expectation that officers and men display courage and, when necessary, risk personal safety to save comrades. Examples provided (Richardson, Sanders, Chalmers) illustrate standards of conduct meriting high decoration. Scoring note: heroism recorded in dispatches and nominations for awards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full recognition of military standing and rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Advocated: give Mounted Police equal rights with members of the permanent Militia in respect of titles, decorations and general standing, including medals, pensions and land grants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative standard: treat mounted police personnel fairly in honors, pensions and other military recognitions when serving on military duty. Practical implication: submit formal appeals/letters (as Steele did) to obtain parity. Anti-pattern: withholding recognition because service was 'on leave' from police.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medical Health Officer duties (comprehensive public‑health remit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dr. Good's summary: (1) inspect hospitals from time to time; (2) see indigents at office or homes and determine hospital admission; (3) inspect the water supply; (4) inspect food and aid in prosecution of those selling food unfit for use; (5) visit vessels arriving and inspect fish, cattle or food before landing; (6) inspect all cattle, sheep and hogs before slaughter to see if they were healthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear, multi‑disciplinary remit for frontier medical officers including sanitary inspection, clinical triage, veterinary checks and public‑health enforcement. Examples: Dawson sanitary program (garbage removal, street cleaning, drainage) shows applied measures. Anti‑pattern: neglecting any of these duties leads to scurvy, typhoid and epidemics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policing with restraint and preservation of life
rubrics_metrics.description: "The Mounted Police know how to use their 'guns,' but they never in all their history degenerated into 'gun‑men.'" and "preserving order without killing anyone where it could be avoided."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethical and operational standard: use force proportionately and prioritize preserving life. Training and discipline should emphasize restraint. Example: Yukon policing where order was maintained without unnecessary killings. Anti‑pattern: turning into 'gun‑men'—overuse of lethal force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal qualities required of frontier policemen
rubrics_metrics.description: When policing immigrant influx and turbulent communities officers must show "consummate tact, endless patience along with unvarying coolness and courage."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recruitment, training and assessment should weigh interpersonal skills, patience, composure under provocation and courage. These social skills are as important as physical prowess for maintaining order in a plural, volatile population.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arctic and long‑range patrol resourcefulness and endurance
rubrics_metrics.description: Patrols often went "in twos and threes and sometimes singly, with nothing beyond their winter and summer uniforms and dependent largely on their own efforts for food"; they faced starvation, sled dogs failing and extreme conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational expectation: patrols must be self‑reliant, minimally equipped, skilled in survival, and able to improvise (e.g., living off game). Reporting should record succinct field observations though accounts are often terse. Anti‑pattern: over‑equipping small patrols with reliance on logistic tails that cannot be sustained in Arctic conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mobile force organisation and wide territorial distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: "Captain Butler's early suggestion... that the men sent out should be a 'mobile force'"; detachments scattered across thousands of miles with one or two men sometimes responsible for vast districts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organisational principle: structure the force for mobility and broad geographic coverage with small detachments capable of rapid response. Deployment planning should account for sparse population and vast distances. Training should emphasize mobility (horse and dog‑train) and local knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equipment and mount standards (re‑armament and logistics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Commissioner Perry: "The Force should be entirely re‑armed." Recommendations include changing from the heavy stock saddle (46 lbs burden), changes in harness, transports and uniforms, and selecting horses "strong in the hindquarters" and appropriate breeding per region.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Logistics standard: modernize arms, lighten soldier loads, adapt saddlery and harness to reduce strain on horses, procure region‑suitable mounts. Practical notes: allow time for training new recruits and horses; procurement must consider long‑term efficiency and animal welfare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thorough, fair and persistent criminal investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: O'Brien murder case: police "wove a web of circumstantial evidence... with consummate skill but with absolute fairness"; investigators pursued the missing man, traced movements, and used painstaking detective work (Constable Pennycuick as 'Sherlock Holmes') even at high expense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigative standard: combine persistence, thorough evidence‑gathering (including circumstantial), fairness and procedural scrupulousness. Authorities should be empowered (expenses granted) to pursue long and difficult inquiries. Example: successful prosecution and high judicial praise for dogged, fair work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public‑health and sanitation leadership in frontier towns
rubrics_metrics.description: Dawson example: garbage removal, specified dumping sites, street cleaning by prison labour, removal of offensive material, and inauguration of drainage—transforming a swamp into a healthier town.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard for local policing/administration: lead or coordinate sanitation campaigns, organize labour for cleaning, set dumping sites, and establish drainage to prevent scurvy/typhoid. Work collaboratively with medical officers and civil authorities. Anti‑pattern: allowing ad hoc filth to persist in boomtowns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protecting vulnerable populations and controlling access to hazardous frontiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Duties included guarding Indians and Esquimaux as wards of the nation, protecting migrants from exploitation, preventing unfit gold‑seekers from venturing into deadly conditions, and controlling approaches to reported oil fields to prevent unprepared people from perishing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mandate: police act as protectors and gatekeepers—manage immigration to hazardous zones, prevent exploitation of indigenous peoples, and restrict access when necessary for safety. Operational measures include cordons, inspections and permitting entry only when properly equipped or under experienced guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of concise official reports documenting extraordinary deeds
rubrics_metrics.description: Field officers "only gave the barest outline of their experience in the reports... but those who know the country could read between the lines and feel the thrill of admiration."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporting standard: even concise official reports are important archival records; officers should submit accurate, if brief, reports recognizing that the Department may bury many details. Ensure key accomplishments and risks are logged so higher authorities can appreciate and act on them (e.g., recognition, resourcing).
